title: Did Christianity Destroy Classical Civilization?
author: The Western Spirit
summary: The Western Spirit rebuts the claim, ancient enough that Augustine's City of God was partly written to answer it, that Christianity destroyed classical Greco-Roman civilization by replacing learning with theology until the Renaissance revived it. Using Augustine's own argument against Rome's pagan defenders after the 410 sack of Rome, that pagan Rome suffered plenty of catastrophic disasters long before Christianity arrived, so blaming Christianity for the city's fall is historically incoherent, the piece shows Augustine mounting this defense while simultaneously demonstrating deep, sustained engagement with Virgil, Cicero, Sallust, Varro, and Plato throughout the same book. The piece's sharpest evidence is biographical: Augustine's own conversion narrative in the Confessions credits Cicero's lost dialogue Hortensius with igniting his lifelong desire for wisdom, years before his conversion to Christianity, a debt Augustine never disowned even after rejecting pagan philosophy wherever it conflicted with Christian truth. St. Basil's counsel to young Christians, extracting what is useful from pagan literature "as in culling roses we avoid the thorns" while guarding against what is harmful, generalizes the argument: far from destroying classical learning, the early Church fathers modeled a deliberate, selective, and sustained engagement with it that shaped Christian civilization from its foundation.
points: Augustine's rebuttal to Rome's pagan defenders is structurally elegant: rather than defending Christianity directly, he redirects the causal question, asking who caused the many catastrophic disasters that struck Rome 'before ever Christ had come in the flesh,' making the accusation self-defeating on its own historical terms.

The piece's strongest evidence against the 'Christianity destroyed classical learning' thesis is that Augustine wrote his defense of Christianity while demonstrating deep, active engagement with Virgil, Cicero, Sallust, Varro, and Plato throughout The City of God itself, the accused destroyer was visibly still reading and using the supposedly destroyed tradition.

The Confessions quotation showing Cicero's lost Hortensius igniting Augustine's 'incredibly burning desire' for wisdom years before his conversion is a precise biographical counterexample: it shows a foundational Christian thinker crediting a specifically pagan text with the philosophical awakening that eventually led him toward Christian faith.

Basil's rose-culling metaphor for engaging pagan literature, take what is useful and true, avoid what is harmful, generalizes Augustine's individual case into an articulated methodology that 'generations of Christian scholars' followed, undercutting the idea that the early Church treated classical learning as something to be discarded wholesale.
quotes: In fact, the accusation is so old that one of the greatest books in Christian history was written partly to answer it.
Augustine's answer was wonderfully simple: if Christianity caused Rome's disasters, who caused all the disasters that came before Christianity?

The Christian bishop supposedly belonging to a religion that destroyed classical learning was sitting in North Africa reading classical authors and using them to write one of the foundational works of Christian civilization.
This book, in truth, changed my affections, and turned my prayers to Thyself, O Lord, and made me have other hopes and desires.
But he never needed to pretend that a pagan author had nothing to teach him simply because he was pagan.

So we, if wise, shall take from heathen books whatever befits us and is allied to the truth, and shall pass over the rest. And just as in culling roses we avoid the thorns, from such writings as these we will gather everything useful, and guard against the noxious.
